title: Britt Prince’s Second Year Leap
text:
Nebraska sophomore guard Britt Prince is in the midst of a breakout season.
The sophomore Omaha native has taken a major leap in her scoring ability from her freshman season, and has shown little signs of slowing down. While not making leaps on her rebounds and assists, Prince’s improvement scoring is incredible.


Code
library(wehoop)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)
library(patchwork)

freshman_data <- load_wbb_player_box(season = 2025)  
sophomore_data <- load_wbb_player_box(season = 2026)

britt_freshman <- freshman_data |>
  filter(athlete_display_name == "Britt Prince") |>
   mutate(season = "2024-25")

britt_sophomore <- sophomore_data |>
  filter(athlete_display_name == "Britt Prince") |>
    mutate(season = "2025-26")

britt_sophomore_fixed <- read_csv("britt_sophomore.csv") |> mutate(athlete_jersey = as.character(athlete_jersey))


freshman_avgs <- britt_freshman |>
  summarise(
    season = "2024-25",
    games = n(),
    ppg = mean(points, na.rm = TRUE),
    rpg = mean(rebounds, na.rm = TRUE),
    apg = mean(assists, na.rm = TRUE),
    spg = mean(steals, na.rm = TRUE),
    bpg = mean(blocks, na.rm = TRUE),
    mpg = mean(minutes, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(ppg, rpg, apg, spg, bpg, mpg), 
               names_to = "statistic", 
               values_to = "value") |>
  filter(statistic %in% c("ppg", "rpg", "apg"))
  

sophomore_avgs <- britt_sophomore_fixed |>
  summarise(
    season = "2025-26", 
    games = n(),
    ppg = mean(points, na.rm = TRUE),
    rpg = mean(rebounds, na.rm = TRUE),
    apg = mean(assists, na.rm = TRUE),
    spg = mean(steals, na.rm = TRUE),
    bpg = mean(blocks, na.rm = TRUE),
    mpg = mean(minutes, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(ppg, rpg, apg, spg, bpg, mpg), 
               names_to = "statistic", 
               values_to = "value") |>
  filter(statistic %in% c("ppg", "rpg", "apg"))

all_players_sophomore <- sophomore_data |>
  group_by(athlete_display_name, athlete_position_name) |>
  summarise(
    games = n(),
    fg_made = sum(field_goals_made, na.rm = TRUE),
    fg_attempted = sum(field_goals_attempted, na.rm = TRUE),
    fg_pct = fg_made / fg_attempted,
    ppg = mean(points, na.rm = TRUE),
    mpg = mean(minutes, na.rm = TRUE),
    apg = mean(assists, na.rm = TRUE),
    rpg = mean(rebounds, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(fg_attempted >= 50, games >= 5)

britt_sophomore_stats <- all_players_sophomore |>
  filter(athlete_display_name == "Britt Prince")


guards_sophomore <- all_players_sophomore |>
  filter(athlete_position_name == "Guard")

freshman_first_8 <- britt_freshman |>
  filter(did_not_play == FALSE) |>
  arrange(game_date) |>
  mutate(
    game_number = row_number(),
    pra = points + rebounds + assists,
    cumul_pra = cumsum(pra)
  ) |>
  filter(game_number <= 8) |>
  mutate(season_label = "Freshman (2024-25)")

sophomore_first_8 <- britt_sophomore_fixed |>
  filter(did_not_play == FALSE) |>
  arrange(game_date) |>
  mutate(
    game_number = row_number(),
    pra = points + rebounds + assists,
    cumul_pra = cumsum(pra)
  ) |>
  filter(game_number <= 8) |>
  mutate(season_label = "Sophomore (2025-26)")

combined_first_8 <- bind_rows(freshman_first_8, sophomore_first_8)

freshman_chart <- ggplot(data = freshman_avgs, aes(x = statistic, y = value)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(value, 1)), vjust = -0.5, size = 4) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,25), breaks = c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20)) + 
  labs(
       x = NULL,
       y = "Per Game Averages") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

sophomore_chart <- ggplot(data = sophomore_avgs, aes(x = statistic, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "red") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(value, 1)), vjust = -0.5, size = 4) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,25), breaks = c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20)) + 
  labs(
       x = NULL,
       y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

freshman_chart + sophomore_chart +
 plot_annotation(
    title = "What a difference a year makes",
    subtitle = "Prince's scoring ability spikes during her sophomore year campaign",
    caption = "Source: wehoop | Camdyn Beirow"
  )  & 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12), 
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size=10),
    ) 









Though the Cornhuskers have not started conference play this season, Britt Prince is averaging eight points per game more than her freshman campaign as a whole, while maintaining her pace of assists per game.
Putting further emphasis on her scoring, Britt Prince is known for slashing and getting to the rim, allowing for more efficient looks at the basket.


Code
ggplot(data = guards_sophomore, aes(x = fg_pct, y = ppg)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = mpg), color = "gray", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = britt_sophomore_stats, 
             aes(x = fg_pct, y = ppg, size = mpg), 
             color = "red", alpha = 1) +
  geom_text_repel(data = britt_sophomore_stats, 
            aes(label = "Britt Prince"),
            vjust = 0.5, size = 4, color = "black", fontface = "bold") +
   geom_vline(xintercept = 0.4024973) + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 11.09659) +
  labs(title = "In a category of her own",
       subtitle = "Prince compared to guards with a minimum of 50 shots attempts and five games played",
       x = "Field Goal Percentage",
       y = "Points Per Game",
       size = "Minutes Per Game",
       caption = "Source: wehoop | Camdyn Beirow") +
  theme_minimal()  + 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12), 
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size=10),
    ) 









Britt Prince is arguably the most efficient guard in all of women’s college basketball. Prince is averaging 21.4 points per game on over 60% shooting from the field. with the average guard in the NCAA averaging 11.1 points per game on 40% shooting, Britt Prince is years ahead of her fellow guards, some who have two full years more experience on her.
Britt Prince statistically speaking is off to a hot start in comparison to her freshman year when comparing her PRA stats (points,rebounds, assists) eight games into each season.


Code
ggplot(data = combined_first_8, aes(x = game_number, y = cumul_pra, 
                            color = season_label, group = season)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Freshman (2024-25)" = "grey", 
                                "Sophomore (2025-26)" = "red")) +
  labs(title = "A step up for Britt Prince",
       subtitle = "PRA (points, rebounds, assists) comapred from Freshman to Sophomore Year",
       x = "Game Number", 
       y = "Cumulative PRA",
       caption = "Source: wehoop | Camdyn Beirow",
       color = "Season") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")  + 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12), 
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size=10)
    ) 









Prince’s sophomore season has seen her accumulate 232 PRA, while her freshman year saw her earn 166 PRA through the first eight games of their respective seasons.The data points to Prince contributing more to the team in her sophomore season than her freshman season. The reasoning behind this is based off of the first to second year jump players take, as well as Prince becoming the first option for the team when Nebraska post Alexis Markowski concluded her final year prior to the 2025-2026 season.
Britt Prince’s second year may very well be marking the start of a remarkable college legecy and a program builder for the Nebraska Cornhuskers. With an incredible scoring leap from year one to two while maintaining her assists per game, Prince could very well be the best guard to go through Nebraska when it is all said and done.

title: Victor Wembanyama and his case for 2026 NBA MVP
text:
Victor Wembanyama is the closest thing to an alien we have ever seen. The French big man stands at 7’4 and is putting up MVP numbers in his third season with the San Antonio Spurs. compared to the former NBA MVPs stats, it appears that Wemby could very well be on pace to win the league’s highest honor if he keeps up or even improves on his stats.
Lets take a peak at some numbers. Hoopr takes and keeps track of NBA data as well as mens college basketball, both player and team stats as well as play-by-play data down to the second.
To start, lets compare Wembanyama’s averages in points, rebounds, and assits in the 2025-2026 season to MVPs of recent years.


Code
library(hoopR)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)


mvp_seasons <- c(2025, 2024, 2023, 2026)

all_data <- load_nba_player_box(seasons =  mvp_seasons)

mvp_comparison_data <- all_data |>
  filter(season_type == 2,
         (athlete_display_name == "Shai Gilgeous-Alexander" & season == 2025) |
         (athlete_display_name == "Nikola Jokic" & season == 2024) |
         (athlete_display_name == "Joel Embiid" & season == 2023) |
         (athlete_display_name == "Victor Wembanyama" & season == 2026))

mvp_avgs <- mvp_comparison_data |>
  group_by(athlete_display_name, season) |>
  summarise(
    games = n(),
    ppg = mean(points, na.rm = TRUE),
    rpg = mean(rebounds, na.rm = TRUE),
    apg = mean(assists, na.rm = TRUE),
    bpg = mean(blocks, na.rm = TRUE),
    spg = mean(steals, na.rm = TRUE),
    minutes = mean(minutes, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

mvp_avgs_long <- mvp_avgs |>
  select(athlete_display_name, season, ppg, rpg, apg) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(ppg, rpg, apg), 
               names_to = "statistic", 
               values_to = "value")

first_10_games <- all_data |>
  filter(season_type == 2,
         (athlete_display_name == "Shai Gilgeous-Alexander" & season == 2025) |
         (athlete_display_name == "Nikola Jokic" & season == 2024) |
         (athlete_display_name == "Joel Embiid" & season == 2023) |
         (athlete_display_name == "Victor Wembanyama" & season == 2026)) |>
  arrange(athlete_display_name, game_date) |>
  group_by(athlete_display_name, season) |>
  filter(row_number() <= 10) |>
  ungroup()

first_10_avgs <- first_10_games |>
  group_by(athlete_display_name, season) |>
  summarise(
    games = n(),
    ppg = mean(points, na.rm = TRUE),
    rpg = mean(rebounds, na.rm = TRUE),
    apg = mean(assists, na.rm = TRUE),
    bpg = mean(blocks, na.rm = TRUE),
    spg = mean(steals, na.rm = TRUE),
    minutes = mean(minutes, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(Player = paste(athlete_display_name, season))

season_2026_data <- load_nba_player_box(seasons = 2026) |>
  filter(season_type == 2)  

player_avgs_2026 <- season_2026_data |>
  group_by(athlete_display_name) |>
  summarise(
    games = n(),
    ppg = mean(points, na.rm = TRUE),
    rpg = mean(rebounds, na.rm = TRUE),
    apg = mean(assists, na.rm = TRUE),
    bpg = mean(blocks, na.rm = TRUE),
    spg = mean(steals, na.rm = TRUE),
    minutes = mean(minutes, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(ppg >= 15 & rpg >= 5)
  
  wemby26avg <- player_avgs_2026 |>
  filter(athlete_display_name == "Victor Wembanyama")
  
  cumulative_stocks <- first_10_games |>
  arrange(athlete_display_name, game_date) |>
  group_by(athlete_display_name, season) |>
  mutate(
    game_number = row_number(),
    stocks = steals + blocks,
    cumulative_stocks = cumsum(stocks)
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(Player = paste(athlete_display_name, season))

fg_pct_minutes <- season_2026_data |>
  group_by(athlete_display_name) |>
  summarise(
    games = n(),
    fg_attempted = sum(field_goals_attempted, na.rm = TRUE),
    fg_made = sum(field_goals_made, na.rm = TRUE),
    fg_pct = fg_made / fg_attempted,
    ppg = mean(points, na.rm = TRUE),
    mpg = mean(minutes, na.rm = TRUE)  
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(fg_attempted >= 50)

wemby_fg_minutes <- fg_pct_minutes |>
  filter(athlete_display_name == "Victor Wembanyama")


ggplot(data= mvp_avgs_long, aes(x = athlete_display_name, y = value, fill = statistic)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "MVP Seasons vs Wembanyama: main three stats comparison",
       x = "Player",
       y = "Per Game Average",
       fill = "Statistic") +
  labs(title = "Welcome to the MVP club?",
       subtitle = "Comparing Wemby to previous MVPs in the 3 major stat categories",
       x = "Points Per Game",
       y = "Rebounds Per Game",
       caption = "By: Camdyn Beirow | Data Source: Hoopr") +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12), 
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size=10)
    ) 









While early into the 2026 season, Wemby’s 26.2 points per game and 12.9 rebounds per game is keeping pace in points per game and rebounds per game with Denver Nuggets center Nikola Jokic’s during his 2024 MVP season. Joel Embiid’s 2023 season only saw him play in 39 games, less than half of the NBA season, potentially boosting his average stats.
But what about Wemby in comparison with his peers in the 2025-2026 campaign?


Code
ggplot(player_avgs_2026, aes(x = ppg, y = rpg))  +
  geom_point(
    data = player_avgs_2026,
    aes(x = ppg, y = rpg), color = "black", alpha = .7
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = wemby26avg,
    aes(x = ppg, y = rpg), color = "red", alpha = 1, size = 3
  ) +
  geom_text(data = wemby26avg, aes(x = 28, y = 13.4, label = "Victor Wembanyama"),
    size = 3
  ) +
  labs(title = "Among Little Company",
       subtitle = "When it comes to scoring and rebounding, wemby is joined by elite few in the modern era",
       x = "Points Per Game",
       y = "Rebounds Per Game",
       caption = "By: Camdyn Beirow | Data Source: Hoopr") +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12), 
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size=10)
    ) 









Looking at the 2026 NBA seasons points per game and rebounds per game, Wemby is exceeding a majority of his peers. Among his peers with a minimum of 15 points per game, wemby sits among the top, sharing the top shelf with Nikola Jokic, who is to his right. In terms of NBA big men, Wembanyama is setting the standard for modern players.
Outside of the main three stats let’s take a look into the defensive end, how does Wemby compare to previous MVPs when it comes to performance on the defensive end?


Code
ggplot(data= cumulative_stocks, aes(x = game_number, y = cumulative_stocks, 
                             color = Player, group = Player)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Wemby's Stock is Through the Roof",
       subtitle = "Wemby's Steals and Blocks, or stocks, stat combo towers among his former MVP peers",
       x = "Games", 
       y = "Cumulative Stocks (Steals + Blocks)",
       caption = "By: Camdyn Beirow | Data Source: Hoopr") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12), 
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size=10)
    ) 









If defense wins championships, then defense must also matter in the MVP discussion. Wemby’s steals and blocks, also known as “stocks”, towers above the previous MVP winners numbers through their first ten games in the season. During his first ten games, Wemby’s single-game high in stocks was 9 against the Brooklyn Nets, while also scoring 31 points on the offensive side. during his 10 game strech, Wemby has more stocks than the last two big men MVP winners combined in that strech.
How does Wemby’s shooting stack up against the league?


Code
ggplot(data= fg_pct_minutes, aes(x = ppg, y = fg_pct)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = mpg), color = "gray", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = wemby_fg_minutes, aes(x = ppg, y = fg_pct, size = mpg), 
             color = "red", alpha = 1) +
  geom_text(data = wemby_fg_minutes, aes(label = "Victor Wembanyama"),
            hjust = -0.1, vjust = 1, size = 3.5, color = "red") +
  geom_smooth(data=fg_pct_minutes, aes(x=ppg, y=fg_pct), method="lm")+
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1, 6)) +
  labs(title = "Efficiency is the name of the game",
       subtitle = "While not the most lights out shooter, Wemby performs well for his role",
       x = "Points Per Game",
       y = "Rebounds Per Game",
       caption = "By: Camdyn Beirow | Data Source: Hoopr") +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12), 
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size=10)
    ) 









Big men historically are not known to shoot the ball well. Victor Wembanyama is apart of the new wave of NBA big men who are able to shoot the ball at an efficient percentage. While not the highest percentage shooter, Wemby is performing well for his amount of points scored per game, shooting above the 50% mark at 50.2% for the 2025-2026 season. While not shooting the lights out, Wemby is performing how you would expect an NBA player with 26.2 ppg, as you can see with the average field goal percentage line based on points per game. When you add in that fact that he is a 7’4 big man who mainly thrives in the paint, his field goal percentage is impresive.
Victor Wembanyama is on the track to grab MVP honors for the first time in his career if he can keep this pace up throughout the 20205-2026 NBA season. Only time will tell if and when we will see “The Alien” earn what is potentially his.
